title: You Have Prepared for Retirement. Have You Prepared Your Heart for Eternity?
paragraphs: You Have Prepared for Retirement. Have You Prepared Your Heart for Eternity?

You may have spent decades preparing for the day you stop working. But Jesus once told a story about a man who prepared brilliantly for the rest of his life—and discovered that the rest of his life was over.
There is something strangely comforting about seeing the numbers finally begin to make sense.
The mortgage is nearly paid.
The children are grown.

There is money tucked away where it is supposed to be. Maybe there is a pension. A retirement account. Insurance. A house that took thirty years to become yours. Perhaps you have already imagined the quieter mornings ahead—the coffee without the alarm clock, the grandchildren visiting, the little trips you kept postponing, the garden you finally have time to tend.
You worked for this.
You sacrificed for this.
You planned for this.
And there is nothing inherently sinful about wise preparation.

Scripture itself commends prudence, diligence, responsible stewardship, providing for one's household, and learning from the ant that prepares its provisions in season. The problem is not that you prepared for tomorrow.
The frightening question is whether tomorrow is the only future you prepared for.
Because there is an appointment on your calendar that your financial adviser cannot reschedule.
There is a journey for which your retirement fund cannot purchase a ticket.
There is a moment when the house, the savings, the investments, the pension, the certificates, the titles, the possessions, and everything bearing your name will remain here...
while you leave.
And Jesus asked a question that reaches through two thousand years and sits down beside us today:
What if you successfully prepare for retirement...
but never prepare your heart for eternity?
Jesus told a story in Luke 12 about a wealthy man whose land produced abundantly.
Notice something important.
Jesus did not say the man stole his harvest.
He did not say he cheated his workers.
He did not say his business was fraudulent.
The ground simply produced so much that the man had a problem most people would love to have.
He had more than he could store.
So he began planning.
“What shall I do?”
His answer sounded sensible.
He would tear down his barns.
Build larger ones.
Store his grain and goods.
Then he would finally relax.
The language becomes painfully revealing when we hear what the man says to himself:
“Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.”
In the Greek text, the word translated “soul” is ψυχή—psychē.
Then God answers him with the same word.
“Fool! This night your soul is required of you.”
Psychē.
Soul.
The very soul the man believed could be satisfied by what was stored in his barns was the one thing his barns could not keep.
That is the tragedy.
He had calculated how much grain he possessed.
He had not calculated how little time he possessed.
He knew the capacity of his barns.
He did not know the date of his death.
He had prepared for “many years.”
God said:
Tonight.
And suddenly the entire story changes.
The bigger barns do not look quite so impressive anymore.
Neither does the balance sheet.
Neither does the property.
Neither does the comfortable future he had rehearsed inside his head.
Because death has a terrifying way of revealing what money can do...
and what money can never do.
Money can buy excellent medical care.
It cannot purchase immortality.
Money can provide a comfortable bed.
It cannot guarantee you will wake up in it tomorrow.
Money can leave an inheritance to your children.
It cannot reconcile your soul to God.
Money can put your name on buildings.
It cannot write your name in the Book of Life.
Money can pay for a funeral.
It cannot pay for a resurrection.
And perhaps that is why this passage feels different when you have lived long enough to realize how quickly life disappears.
When you were twenty-five, seventy seemed impossibly far away.
Then somehow the years started accelerating.
Thirty became forty.
Forty became fifty.
The children who once needed you to tie their shoes began raising children of their own.
Friends started getting sick.
Some names disappeared from your Christmas list because those people were no longer here.
One day you looked into a mirror and saw traces of your parents looking back at you.
You began attending more funerals than weddings.
And perhaps, quietly, mortality stopped being a theological concept.
It became personal.
Maybe you do not fear death.
Maybe you simply avoid thinking about it.
There is always another distraction.
Another television program.
Another vacation.
Another project around the house.
Another appointment.
Another family gathering.
Another year.
But beneath all the noise sits the question most human beings eventually have to face:
When my heart beats for the final time...
what happens to me?
Jesus does not allow us to answer that question with our bank statement.
At the end of the parable, He says that this is what happens to the person who stores up treasure for himself but is not “rich toward God.”
That phrase matters.

Jesus was not teaching that possessing money automatically condemns a person. Scripture contains faithful people who possessed material wealth, and it repeatedly calls believers to generosity, stewardship, contentment, justice, and care for others.
The deeper disease in Luke 12 is revealed by one devastating absence.
Listen again to the rich man's plans.
My crops.
My barns.
My grain.
My goods.
My soul.
My future.
There is plenty of “my.”
There is almost no God.
That is why this story is not merely about wealthy people.
It is about us.
You can have very little money and still build your entire existence around yourself.
You can also possess much and hold it with open hands before God.
The issue reaches deeper than the size of the account.
What owns your heart?
What are you trusting?
What have you quietly asked to give you the security only God can give?
Because the greatest retirement danger is not running out of money before you die.
It is reaching death without Christ.
And that sentence may sting.
It should.
Not because Jesus delights in frightening people, but because He loves people too much to flatter them about eternity.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Become religious enough before you die.”
It is not God demanding that you accumulate enough good deeds to outweigh the bad ones.
It is not a celestial retirement account where sufficient moral deposits eventually purchase heaven.
That would leave every one of us bankrupt.
Scripture says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
All.
The respectable grandfather.
The devoted grandmother.
The successful businessman.
The church volunteer.
The person who has attended Sunday worship for fifty years.
The person who has not entered a church since childhood.
You.
Me.
Sin is not merely the scandalous thing somebody else did.

It is our rebellion against the God who made us. It is the pride we excused. The bitterness we fed. The lust we hid. The forgiveness we withheld. The lies nobody discovered. The selfishness we renamed “wisdom.” The years we lived as though God were a supporting character in a story that belonged to us.
And eventually the question becomes unavoidable.
If my money cannot save me...
if my accomplishments cannot save me...
if my reputation cannot save me...
if even my religious résumé cannot save me...
then who can?
Jesus.
That is where the story turns from scandal to grace.
Because the same Christ who warned about the rich fool went willingly toward a cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, did what we could never do. He lived without sin. He gave Himself for sinners. He bore judgment at the cross. He died, was buried, and rose again.
The answer to death was not hidden inside a bigger barn.
It walked out of an empty tomb.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately a strategy for becoming a nicer person before you die.
It is news.
Good news.
Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Reconciliation with God is found in Him.
Eternal life is found in Him.
The Greek word so often translated “repent” is μετανοέω—metanoeō—carrying the sense of turning, of a changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to Christ.
That distinction matters enormously because it is possible to spend decades around Christianity without surrendering to Christ.
You can know the hymns.
Know when to stand.
Know when to sit.
Know the Christmas story.
Know the Easter story.
Own three Bibles.
Have a favorite preacher.
Call yourself Christian.
And still quietly trust your morality, your church attendance, your generosity, your family heritage, or the fact that you were “never as bad as other people.”
But eternity is too important for borrowed faith.
Your spouse cannot believe for you.
Your parents cannot believe for you.
Your pastor cannot believe for you.
Your children cannot believe for you.
And the fact that you intend to deal with God “someday” should make Luke 12 thunder in your ears.
The rich man had a someday too.
He planned many years.
God said tonight.
None of us knows when our “tonight” will come.
This is not a prediction about when you will die.
It is simply the reality Jesus refuses to let us escape:
Life is uncertain.
Eternity is not something we should postpone preparing for.
Perhaps you have already prepared documents telling your family what to do when you are gone.
You chose beneficiaries.
You wrote a will.
You arranged insurance.
You told someone where the important papers are.
You may even have discussed what kind of funeral you want.
Those can be loving and responsible decisions.
But there is a question infinitely more important than who receives what you leave behind.
Who has your soul?
Maybe that question exposed something.
Maybe there is an old sin you have carried for decades.
Something nobody knows.
Something you believed disqualified you from ever coming home to God.
An affair.
An abortion.
A betrayal.
An addiction.
A season of abandoning your family.
Years of anger.
Years of hypocrisy.
Years of pretending.
Maybe everyone thinks you are the strong Christian in the family, but privately you know how far your heart has wandered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is for sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not impressive sinners.
Not sinners who have successfully erased their history.
Sinners.
That is why grace is grace.
Your past may explain some of your scars, but it does not possess greater authority than the blood of Christ.

There are consequences in this life that repentance does not magically erase. There may be apologies that still need to be made, restitution that should be pursued where possible, relationships that may never return to what they once were.
But no history of sin is stronger than Christ's sufficiency to save those who come to Him.
This is our message:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never happened.
He rewrites what your sin gets to say about your eternity.
The cross says your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
The empty tomb says death does not get the final word.
Grace says you do not have to hide anymore.
Maybe you have spent your entire adult life providing for everybody else.
You made sure your children had food.
You paid tuition.
You worked overtime.
You cared for aging parents.
You carried responsibilities nobody noticed.
You saved what you could.
You built something for the next generation.
There is dignity in faithful provision.
But after taking care of everybody else's future...
do not neglect your own soul.
Your greatest legacy will never be the amount of money your children receive when you die.
The greatest inheritance you can leave is a life that points beyond itself to Jesus Christ.
Let your children remember that Dad loved Jesus.
Let your grandchildren remember that Grandma prayed.
Let them remember seeing repentance instead of pride.
Let them remember forgiveness.
Let them remember generosity.
Let them remember that when your body became weaker, your hope became clearer.
Let them watch you demonstrate that Christ is better than everything this world eventually takes away.
Because eventually, if we live long enough, earthly things begin slipping from our hands.
Strength changes.
Health changes.
Appearance changes.
Careers end.
Titles disappear.
Possessions pass to somebody else.
Homes are sold.
Closets are emptied.
Someone eventually sorts through boxes containing the objects we once considered indispensable.
But the Christian's hope was never supposed to be that we could hold onto this world forever.
Our hope is Christ.
Paul could therefore speak of death in a way that makes no sense apart from Jesus: “to die is gain.”
Gain?
Only if what waits beyond death is better than what death takes away.
Only if Christ is there.
Only if resurrection is real.
Only if the Gospel is true.
And Christianity stands or falls on that astonishing announcement: Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
So prepare wisely for retirement.
Save responsibly.
Make a will.
Take care of your spouse.
Be generous.
Enjoy God's gifts with gratitude.
Hold your grandchildren.
Travel if you are able.
Sit beside the ocean.
Plant tomatoes.
Laugh around the dinner table.
Thank God for ordinary mornings.
But never confuse preparing to stop working with preparing to meet God.
Your retirement may last thirty years.
It may last three.
You may never reach it.
Eternity is longer.
And perhaps the most important thing you can do after reading this is not check your retirement account again.
Perhaps it is close the door.
Turn off the noise.
Sit somewhere alone.
And stop pretending with God.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Drop the religious performance.
Turn to Jesus Christ.
Do not trust a prayer as though certain words were magical. Trust the Savior to whom you are praying.
“Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Make me Yours. Teach me to follow You for whatever days You give me.”
If that reflects what is truly happening in your heart, do not bury this moment beneath tomorrow's routine.
Open Scripture.
Read the Gospel of John.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church where Christ and His Gospel are proclaimed.
Tell another mature Christian that you have turned to Christ and need help learning to follow Him.
And if you have followed Jesus for years, perhaps this is your reminder that retirement from a career is not retirement from the Kingdom of God.
As long as God gives you breath, there are people to love.
People to forgive.
People to encourage.
People to disciple.
People who need to hear what Christ has done.
There are prayers your grandchildren desperately need somebody to pray.
There are younger believers who need the wisdom you paid decades to acquire.
There are wounded people who may listen to you precisely because you have scars too.
Finish well.
Not impressively.
Faithfully.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not—but because someone you know may have spent forty years preparing financially for retirement without seriously considering eternity.
Send it privately to the brother who does not like talking about death.
Send it to the sister who has everything prepared except the conversation she keeps avoiding with God.
One share cannot save a soul.
Jesus saves.
But one share can put the Gospel in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own heart, do not hide behind silence here either.
Or simply tell your story. Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person who has struggled, wandered, repented, returned, and found mercy in Christ.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient, loving lives—not through a transaction.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, gratefully, and for God's glory.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your sin.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ.

So when the final night eventually comes—and the plans are finished, the accounts no longer matter, the house belongs to someone else, and the world continues without us—may our confidence not be, “I stored enough.”
May it be:
Christ is enough.
You spent years making sure you would have enough to live on when your work was finished; make certain you know the One who conquered death when your life is finished.
